doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

chapter: Bass playing, avant-garde and the state of the music
title: Labels, big business and the term jazz
summary: Ware says new labels like bebop and rock sell berets and blue jeans, and Gloria notes the music existed before the label.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: It's always a new sound. Jazz and rock.
Well, why is it necessary, do you think, to categorize in that way?

Well, big business, you know. It's just like, you say, this is new, this is something new. When what they say be-bop come out, they was able to sell a whole lot of berets and horn-rimmed glasses. Big business. Economics. Rock, they were able to sell a whole lot of blue jeans.

But it's as though the thing itself exists and the exploitation of the thing is labeled. You know what I mean? Like the music existed. People used it and start playing it and call it Dixieland, but it already existed before that.
Before the label was tacked onto it.

Or exploited. It's funny when you talk about accepting, which may be part of the problem. Over the years, you see people ask for acceptance, in a sense, like Rahsaan. He was involved in that. People want to get exposed in music and get on television and so forth, but accepting it on different terms, because as far as people, if you look in the Encyclopedia Brittanica or you look up the word jazz, it will say something to the effect that it started in the black experience and it's now American music. That's a point of view. That's an American point of view.
So that when they see Benny Goodman and call him the King --
